cues.text: A Pope Committed to Reunion
Elected in 1271 after a papal vacancy of nearly three years, Pope Gregory X had served as a churchman in the Holy Land.
He returned to Europe convinced that healing the two-century-old rift with the Greek Church and mounting a new crusade were Christendom’s most urgent tasks.
He summoned a general council to meet at Lyon , the same city that had hosted Innocent IV's council against Frederick II a generation earlier, to pursue both goals together.
The council opened on May 7, 1274 and drew an extraordinary assembly of some five hundred bishops and sixty abbots.
It also included well over a thousand other prelates and procurators, alongside King James I of Aragon and ambassadors of the kings of France and England.
Byzantine Overtures
The Byzantine emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos had strong political reasons of his own to seek reconciliation with Rome.

Having recaptured Constantinople from the Latin crusader states in 1261, he saw reunion as a way to remove the pretext for a Western crusade against his restored empire, particularly from the ambitious Charles of Anjou , King of Sicily.

Michael sent letters accepting papal primacy and dispatched a delegation led by the former Patriarch Germanus and the theologian-diplomat Georgius Acropolita , which arrived at Lyon on June 24, 1274, after a difficult voyage that nearly ended in shipwreck.
On the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, June 29, Gregory X celebrated Mass with the Greek delegation.
The Nicene Creed, including the contested filioque clause describing the Holy Spirit as proceeding from the Father and the Son, was sung three times in Greek as well as Latin.
The Act of Union

In the fourth session, held on July 6, 1274, the council formally proclaimed the union of the Greek and Latin Churches, with the Greek delegates accepting Roman primacy and the Latin teaching on the procession of the Holy Spirit.
It was the first time the Western Church had formally required acceptance of the filioque as a matter of dogma.
The doctrine had itself been one of the primary points of theological division between East and West since the eleventh century.

The council also addressed reform of papal elections, establishing rules for the conclave requiring cardinals to be sequestered until they reached a decision, a procedural reform still echoed in the elaborate secrecy of papal conclaves today.
A Union Without Support
The union proclaimed at Lyon rested on remarkably thin foundations in the East.
Emperor Michael VIII had negotiated it almost entirely for political reasons, with little consultation.
The wider Byzantine clergy and laity were mostly excluded, and the great majority deeply opposed submission to Rome and rejection of their own liturgical and theological traditions.
Resistance in Constantinople was immediate and fierce, and Michael was forced to resort to persecution of anti-unionist monks and clergy to enforce the agreement during his lifetime.

When Michael died in 1282, his son and successor Andronikos II promptly repudiated the union altogether, and the reconciliation collapsed entirely, leaving the schism between Rome and Constantinople as unresolved as before.
Legacy

Second Lyon remains, alongside the later Council of Florence, one of two medieval attempts at reunion between the Greek and Latin Churches that achieved formal, conciliar agreement only to unravel within a generation once the underlying political motivations faded.
Its brief union nonetheless stands as an important precedent in the long history of Catholic-Orthodox dialogue.

It demonstrated that reunion on paper was achievable, yet showed how difficult it proved to translate diplomatic agreement into durable reconciliation between two distinct ecclesial traditions and their peoples.
